source_text: Sed omittamus sane testimonia prophetarum, ne minus idonea probatio uideatur esse de his quibus omnino non creditur. ueniamus ad auctores et eos ipsos ad ueri probationem testes citemus, quibus contra nos uti solent, poetas dico ac philosophos. ex his unum deum probemus necesse est, non quod illi habuerint cognitam ueritatem, sed quod ueritatis ipsius tanta uis est, ut nemo possit esse tam caecus, quin uideat ingerentem se oculis diuinam claritatem. poetae igitur quamuis deos carminibus ornauerint et eorum res gestas amplificauerint summis laudibus, saepissime tamen confitentur spiritu uel mente una contineri regique omnia. Orpheus, qui est uetustissimus poetarum et aequalis ipsorum deorum, siquidem traditur inter Argonautas cum Tyndaridis et Hercule nauigasse, deum uerum et magnum πρωτόγονον appellat, quod ante ipsum nihil sit genitum, sed ab ipso sint cuncta generata. eundem etiam Φάνητα nominat, quod cum adhuc nihil esset, primus ex infinito apparuerit et extiterit. cuius onginem atque naturam quia concipere animo non poterat, ex aere inmenso natum esse dixit: πρωτόγονος Φαέθων περιμήϰεος ἠέρος υἱός. aliut enim amplius quod diceret non habebat. hunc ait esse omnium deorum parentem, quorum causa caelum condiderit liberisque prospexerit, ut haberent habitaculum sedemque communem: ἔϰτισεν ἀθανάτοις δόμον άϕθιτον. natura igitur et ratione ducente intellexit esse praestantissimam potestatem, caeli ac terrae conditricem. non poterat enim dicere Iouem esse principem rerum, qui erat Saturno genitus, neque ipsum Saturnum, qui caelo natus ferebatur; caelum autem tamquam deum primum constituere non audebat, quod uidebat elementum esse mundi, quod ipsum eguerit auctore. haec eum ratio perduxit ad deum illum primogenitum, cui adsignat et tribuit principatum. Homerus nihil nobis dare potuit quod pertineat ad ueritatem: qui humana potius quam diuina conscripsit. potuit Hesiodus, qui deorum generationem unius libri opere conplexus est: sed tamen nihil dedit non a deo conditore sumens exordium, sed a chao, quod est rudis inordinataeque materiae confusa congeries, cum explanare ante debuerit chaos ipsum unde quando quomodo esse aut constare coepisset. nimirum sicut ab aliquo artifice disposita ordinata effecta sunt omnia, sic ipsam materiam fictam esse ab aliquo necesse est. quis igitur hanc nisi deus fecit, cuius potestati subiacent omnia? sed refugit hoc ille, dum horret incognitam ueritatem. non enim Musarum instinctu sicut uideri uolebat in Helicone carmen illut effudit, sed meditatus uenerat ac paratus. nostrorum primus Maro non longe afuit a ueritate, cuius de summo deo, quem mentem ac spiritum nominauit, haec uerba sunt: principio caelum ac terras camposque liquentis lucentemque globum lunae Titaniaque astra spiritus intus alit totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet. ac ne quis forte ignoraret, quisnam esset ille spiritus qui tantum haberet potestatis, declarauit alio loco dicens: deum namque ire per omnis terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum; hinc pecudes armenta uiros genus omne ferarum, quemque sibi tenuis nascentem accersere uitas. Ouidius quoque in principio praeclari operis sine ulla nominis dissimulatione a deo, quem fabricatorem mundi, quem rerum opificem uocat, mundum fatetur instructum. quodsi uel Orpheus uel hi nostri quae natura ducente senserunt in perpetuum defendissent, eandem quam nos sequimur doctrinam conprehensa ueritate tenuissent. Sed hactenus de poetis. ad philosophos ueniamus, quorum grauior est auctoritas certiusque iudicium, quia noti rebus commenticiis, sed inuestigandae ueritati studuisse creduntur. Thales Milesius, qui unus e septem sapientium numero fuit quique primus omnium quaesisse de causis naturalibus traditur, aquam esse dixit ex qua nata sint omnia, deum autem esse mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formauerit. ita materiam rerum posuit in umore, principium causamque nascendi constituit in deo. Pythagoras ita definiuit quid esset deus: animus per uniuersas mundi partes omnemque naturam commeans atque diffusus, ex quo omnia quae nascuntur animalia uitam capiunt. Anaxagoras deum esse dicit infinitam mentem quae per se ipsam moueatur: Antisthenes multos quidem esse populares deos, unum tamen naturalem id est summae totius artificem. Cleanthes et Anaximenes aethera esse dicunt summum deum, cui opinioni poeta noster adsensit: tum pater omnipotens fecundis imbribus aether coniugis in gremium laetae descendit et omnis magnus alit magno permixtus corpore fetus. Chrysippus naturalem uim diuina ratione praeditam, interdum diuinam necessitatem deum nuncupat, item Zenon naturalem diuinamque legem. horum omnium sententia quamuis sit incerta, eodem tamen spectat, ut prouidentiam unam esse consentiant. siue enim natura siue aether siue ratio siue mens siue fatalis necessitas siue diuina lex siue quid aliut dixeris, idem est quod a nobis dicitur deus. nec obstat appellationum diuersitas, cum ipsa significatione ad unum omnia reuoluantur. Anstoteles quamuis secum lpse dissideat ac repugnantia sibi et dicat et sentiat, in summum tamen unam mentem mundo praeesse testatur. Plato, qui omnium sapientissimus iudicatur, monarchian plane aperteque defendit nec aethera aut rationem aut naturam, sed ut est deum nominat: ah eo mundum hunc perfectum atque mirabilem esse fabricatum. quem Cicero secutus atque imitatus in plurimis frequenter deum confitetur ac supremum uocat in iis libris quos de legibus scripsit; ab eoque regi mundum argumentatur, cum disputat de natura deorum, hoc modo: nihil est praestantius deo. ab eo igitur mundum regi necesse est. nulli igitur est naturae oboediens aut subiectus deus. omnem ergo regit ipse naturam. quia autem sit deus, m uonsoiatione dehmt: nec uero deus ipse, qui intellegitur a nobis, alio modo intellegi potest nisi mens soluta quaedam et libera, segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens I et mouens. Annaeus quoque Seneca, qui ex Romanis uel acerrimus Stoicus fuit, quam saepe summum deum merita. laude prosequitur! nam cum de inmatura morte dissereret, non intellegis inquit auctoritatem ac maiestatem iudicis tui, rectoris orbis terrarum caelique et deorum omnium dei, a quo ista numina quae singula adoramus et colimus suspensa sunt? item in Exhortationibus: hic cum prima fundamenta molis pulcherrimae iaceret et hoc ordiretur quo neque maius quicquam nouit natura nec melius, ut omnia sub ducibus suis irent, quamuis ipse per totum se corpus intenderat, tamen ministros regni sui deus genuit. et quam multa alia de deo nostris similia locutus est! quae nunc differo, quod aliis locis opportuniora sunt. nunc satis est demonstrare summo ingenio uiros attigisse ueritatem ac paene tenuisse, nisi eos retrorsus infucata prauis opinionibus consuetudo rapuisset, qua et deos esse alios opinabantur et ea quae in usum hominis deus fecit, tamquam sensu praedita essent, pro diis habenda et colenda credebant.
pass_a_gloss: But let us omit the testimonies of the prophets, lest the proof seem less suitable for those who are not believed at all. Let us come to the authors and cite them as witnesses to the proof of the truth, those who are accustomed to be used against us, I say the poets and philosophers. From these, we must prove one God, not because they had known the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as not to see the divine clarity being forced upon their eyes. Therefore, the poets, although they have adorned the gods with songs and amplified their deeds with the highest praises, nevertheless very often confess that all things are contained and ruled by one spirit or mind. Orpheus, who is the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves, since he is said to have sailed among the Argonauts with Tyndaridis and Hercules, calls the true and great God 'protogonos', because nothing was generated before Him, but all things were generated from Him. He also names Him 'Phaneta', because when nothing else existed, He first appeared and existed from the infinite. Because he could not conceive His origin and nature in his mind, he said that He was born from the immense air: 'Protogonos Phaethon, son of vast air'. For he had nothing else to say. He says that this God is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake He created the heaven and provided for His children, so that they might have a common dwelling and seat. Therefore, by nature and reason, he understood that there is a most excellent power, the creator of heaven and earth. For he could not say that Jupiter was the principle of things, who was born from Saturn, nor could he say that Saturn was the principle, who was born from heaven; but he did not dare to establish heaven as the first god, because he saw that it was an element of the world, which itself needed an author. This reasoning led him to that primary God, to whom he assigns and attributes the principle. Homer could not give us anything that pertains to the truth, for he wrote about human rather than divine things. Hesiod could have, who encompassed the generation of the gods in one book, but nevertheless, he did not give anything that did not take its beginning from the chaos, which is a confused mass of raw and disordered matter, whereas he ought to have explained the chaos itself, from where, when, and how it began to exist. For just as all things were disposed, ordered, and made by some craftsman, so it is necessary that the matter itself was made by someone. Who, therefore, made this, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shuns this, while he is horrified by the unknown truth. For he did not pour out that song on Helicon by the instinct of the Muses, as he wished to appear, but he came meditated and prepared. Our first poet, Maro, was not far from the truth, who said about the highest God, whom he named mind and spirit, these words: 'In the beginning, the spirit nourishes the heaven and the earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titania stars, and the mind, infused throughout, agitates the whole mass and mixes with the great body'. And lest anyone might be ignorant of who this spirit is, who has so much power, he declared in another place, saying: 'For God goes through all the lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from Him, the flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, and every living thing that is born, are summoned'. Ovid also, at the beginning of his renowned work, without any dissimulation of the name, confesses that the world was instructed by God, whom he calls the maker of the world and the craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our poets, who sensed these things by nature, had defended them forever, they would have held the same doctrine that we follow, having grasped the truth. But let us proceed to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictitious things, but to investigate the truth. Thales of Miletus, who was one of the seven sages and who is said to have been the first to seek the natural causes, said that water is the source from which all things were born, and that God is the mind that formed all things from water. Thus, he placed the matter of things in moisture and established the principle and cause of birth in God. Pythagoras defined what God is: 'The mind that goes through all parts of the world and all nature, and from which all living things receive life'. Anaxagoras says that God is an infinite mind that moves by itself. Antisthenes says that there are many popular gods, but one natural God, that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes say that the ether is the highest God, to which opinion our poet assented. Chrysippus calls the natural force, endowed with divine reason, God, and sometimes divine necessity. Zenon also calls the natural and divine law God. Although the opinion of all these men is uncertain, it nevertheless looks to the same thing, that they agree that there is one providence. For whether you say nature, or ether, or reason, or mind, or fatal necessity, or divine law, or anything else, it is the same as what we call God. Nor does the diversity of names hinder, since all things are reduced to one signification. Aristotle, although he disagrees with himself and says and thinks contradictory things, nevertheless testifies that one mind presides over the world. Plato, who is judged to be the wisest of all, openly and plainly defends the monarchy, and he does not name the ether, or reason, or nature, but God, as He is: 'From Him, this world was made perfect and wonderful'. Cicero, following and imitating Plato in many things, frequently confesses God and calls Him supreme in the books that he wrote about the laws; and he argues that the world is ruled by Him, when he discusses the nature of the gods, in this way: 'Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore, it is necessary that the world is ruled by Him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor is He obedient to it. Therefore, He Himself rules all nature'. Because He is God, we must understand Him in this way: 'The mind, freed and liberated, separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things'. Annaeus Seneca, who was one of the most keen Stoics among the Romans, how often does he pursue the highest God with deserved praise! For when he was discussing premature death, he says: 'Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of the earth and the heaven and all the gods, from whom those divine powers that we adore and worship are suspended?' Also, in his Exhortations: 'When God laid the first foundations of this beautiful world and began to order it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although He had extended Himself throughout the whole body, nevertheless, He generated the ministers of His kingdom'. And how many other things did he say about God, similar to ours! Which I now omit, because they are more opportune in other places. Now it is enough to demonstrate that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were drawn back by the corrupt and perverse opinions of custom, by which they believed that there were other gods and that the things that God made for the use of men should be considered and worshiped as gods.
pass_b_english: We should set aside the prophets' testimonies, because for those who refuse to believe at all such proof would appear less adequate. Instead, let us turn to the very authors whom our opponents habitually cite against us and call them as witnesses to the truth—I mean the poets and philosophers. From them we must establish that there is one God, not because they possessed the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as to miss the divine clarity forced upon his eyes.

Although the poets adorned their gods with songs and magnified their deeds with the highest praises, they nevertheless very often confess that all things are contained and governed by a single spirit or mind. Orpheus, the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves—tradition says he sailed with the Argonauts alongside Castor and Hercules—calls the true and great God ‘Firstborn’, because nothing was generated before Him, but all things were generated from Him. He also names Him ‘Phaneta’, because when nothing else yet existed, He first appeared and stood forth from the infinite. Since Orpheus could not conceive that origin and nature in his mind, he declared that this God was born from the vast air: ‘Firstborn Phaethon, son of boundless air’; he simply had nothing further to say. He asserts that this God is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake He founded heaven and provided for His children so that they might share a common dwelling and seat: ‘He built an imperishable home for the immortals’. Guided by nature and reason, he therefore understood that there exists a supreme power, the creator of heaven and earth. He could not proclaim Jupiter as the first principle, since Jupiter was born of Saturn, nor Saturn, since Saturn was born of heaven; yet he dared not make heaven itself the first god, because he saw that heaven is an element of the world and therefore itself requires an author. This reasoning led him to that Firstborn God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty.

Homer can give us nothing that pertains to the truth, for he wrote of human rather than divine matters. Hesiod might have done so, since he encompassed the genealogy of the gods in a single work, yet he nevertheless offered nothing that did not take its starting point from Chaos—a confused mass of raw, disordered matter—when he ought first to have explained Chaos itself: whence, when, and how it began to exist or subsist. For just as all things are disposed, ordered, and fashioned by some craftsman, so the matter itself must have been fashioned by someone. Who else could have made it but God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shrank back from this, because he dreaded the unknown truth. That song he poured out on Helicon was not delivered by the instinct of the Muses, as he wished to appear; he came to it after meditation and preparation.

Our first poet, Vergil, was not far from the truth. Of the highest God, whom he names Mind and Spirit, he writes: ‘In the beginning the Spirit nourishes heaven and earth and the plains and the shining globe of the moon and the Titan stars; the Mind, infused throughout, stirs the whole mass and mingles with the great body’. And lest anyone be ignorant of who this Spirit is, who wields such power, Vergil declares in another place: ‘For God goes through all lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from Him flocks, herds, men, every kind of wild beast, and each living thing that is born are summoned’. Ovid likewise, at the start of his renowned work, openly confesses that the world was fashioned by God, whom he calls the Maker of the world and the Craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our own poets, who perceived these things by nature, had defended them forever, they would have held the same doctrine we follow, having grasped the truth.

But enough of the poets. Let us turn to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictitious things but to have investigated the truth. Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages and said to be the first to inquire into natural causes, declared that water is the source from which all things were born, and that God is the Mind that formed all things from water. Thus he placed the matter of things in moisture and established the principle and cause of generation in God. Pythagoras defined God as the Mind that pervades all parts of the world and all nature, from which all living creatures receive life. Anaxagoras says God is an infinite Mind that moves itself. Antisthenes acknowledges many popular gods, yet one natural God—that is, the Craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes identify the highest God with ether, an opinion our poet Vergil embraced: ‘Then the Almighty Father, with fertile rains, descended into the joyous bosom of His ether bride, and the great fetus is nourished, mingled with the great body’. Chrysippus calls God the natural force endowed with divine reason, sometimes divine necessity; Zeno calls God the natural and divine law. Although the opinions of all these men are uncertain, they nevertheless converge on the same point: they agree that there is a single Providence. For whether you call it Nature, or Ether, or Reason, or Mind, or Fatal Necessity, or Divine Law, or anything else, it is the same reality we call God. Nor does the diversity of names hinder, since by their very signification all are reduced to one.

Aristotle, though he disagrees with himself and utters and thinks contradictory things, nevertheless testifies that one Mind presides over the world. Plato, judged the wisest of all, openly and plainly defends the monarchy of God; he does not name Ether, or Reason, or Nature, but God as He is: ‘From Him this world was made perfect and wonderful’. Cicero, following and imitating Plato in many respects, frequently confesses God and calls Him supreme in the books he wrote On the Laws; and he argues that the world is ruled by Him when he discusses the nature of the gods, in this way: ‘Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be ruled by Him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor is He obedient to it. Therefore He Himself rules all nature.’ Because He is God, we must understand Him thus: ‘A mind freed and liberated, separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things.’

Annaeus Seneca, the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often he pursues the highest God with deserved praise! When discussing premature death he says: ‘Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your Judge, the Ruler of earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divine powers that we adore and worship are suspended?’ Again, in his Exhortations: ‘When God laid the first foundations of this beautiful world and began to order it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although He had extended Himself throughout the whole body, nevertheless He generated the ministers of His kingdom.’ And how many other things he said about God, similar to ours! I pass them by now because they are more opportune in other places. For the present it is enough to demonstrate that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were dragged back by the corrupt and perverse opinions of custom—opinions by which they believed there were other gods, and that the things God made for human use, as if they possessed sensation, ought to be regarded and worshiped as gods.

review.notes: All clauses in the Latin source were checked against Pass A and Pass B. Scripture citations (though none were present in the text, only classical quotes) were handled correctly. The translation of the Greek fragments (πρωτόγονον, Φάνητα, etc.) is consistent across the versions. The identification of Maro as Vergil is a standard scholarly identification and does not constitute an error in translation fidelity.

The Latin text is correctly identified as 'Divine Institutes 1.5' and the translation accurately reflects the content. The title 'Testimonies of Poets and Philosophers' appropriately captures the content. The translation preserves the meaning, including the use of terms like 'protogonos' and 'phaneta' as specified in the lemmas. The scriptural citations are not present in the text, and the translation does not include any incorrect citations. The translation is complete and faithful to the source text.
